title: Three births: the third is death
hook: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying

segments.voice: Yesterday: vidriti, atman: the one who sees through every door of the head, where the self, atman, came in and said, I have seen this.

How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID. Ask a family and it gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming. And in some families there's a day after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya's second chapter counts births too. It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.
screen: `HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?` → `THE DAY SOMEONE FOUND OUT.` → `THE AITAREYA COUNTS THREE.`

segments.voice: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father. The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second. The child becomes one with the mother, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn. The father cares for the child before birth and after, and so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third. The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old and departs. And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Here is a core Hindu teaching in one line: death isn't the opposite of birth. It's the next one. The self goes on, and the tradition surrounds that crossing with care. The funeral rite is called antyeshti, the last offering, and in the days and years after, families make shraddha offerings for those who have gone ahead. Then the chapter turns to a seer, Vamadeva, and quotes his verse from the Rig Veda: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out. So when a Hindu family says someone has passed on, they mean on.
screen: `THE FIRST BIRTH: IN THE FATHER.` · `THE SECOND: FROM THE MOTHER.` · `THE THIRD: DEPARTING, BORN AGAIN.` · `ANTYESHTI: THE LAST OFFERING.` · then, large: `DYING IS THE THIRD BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Let one breath go to the people who carried you before you were born, whoever held the hope of you, and one to those who fed and held you before you could thank them. Then, gently, think of someone who has died; in the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are.

Vamadeva, the seer who said, while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. The Aitareya counts three births: conception in the father, birth from the mother, and death, when a person departs and is born again.
Take this with you: dying is the third birth. Tomorrow, the Aitareya's last chapter asks who the self is. That's day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

chat.meaning: The Aitareya counts three births: in the father, from the mother, and the third when a parent departs and is born again. Hindu funeral and shraddha rites send the departed on.

Vamadeva.meaning: a Rig Veda seer who knew the gods' births from the womb

Rig Veda.meaning: the oldest of the four Vedas

Aitareya.meaning: a short Upanishad of the Rig Veda

antyeshti.meaning: the Hindu funeral rite: the last offering

shraddha.meaning: offerings families make for those who have died (a different word from shraddha, faith)

notes: Aitareya 2.1–4 paraphrased from memory, including 'she doesn't harm it' (na himsati) and 'she is to be nourished' (sa bhavayitri bhavayitavya bhavati). Confirm.
Verse numbering: the Aitareya's second chapter is often printed as one section (2.1) with sub-verses 1–6; the Vamadeva verse is cited as 2.5 here. Confirm.
The text's account is framed around the father; the script keeps that while giving the mother's verse its weight. A Keeper may want to frame this more.
The fork's distractor 'initiation' alludes to the separate idea of the twice-born (upanayana), not taught here.
